messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir was seven years old the first time he saw his father’s fist connect with his mother’s jaw. The memory that stayed—the one that came back like a photograph, each detail fixed and frozen—was not the blow itself but the moment just after: his mother’s head turning slowly, her eyes finding his across the kitchen, and the look that said *don’t say a word*. Other parts of that night had vanished entirely—how they got to the hospital, what his father said afterward—but that single image was stamped into him, as clear and still as a picture on a wall. He learned quickly that conflict meant danger, that authority figures like his father could erupt without warning, and that the safest response was to disappear inside himself.

As an adult, Amir worked construction, a job that kept his hands busy and his mind elsewhere—except that the job site was full of the very things he had spent decades trying to avoid. A foreman’s raised voice on a Monday morning sent a bolt of heat through his chest; his heart hammered, his palms went cold, and he found himself scanning the man’s face for the flicker of something worse. He had come to believe that people’s expressions held hidden threats, so he watched their mouths and brows the way he had once watched his father’s hands. When a coworker asked him what he planned to do next year, Amir’s mind went blank, then swerved sharply into the past—he would dwell on the boy he had been before that night, the one who had not yet learned to brace for impact. Talking about the future felt like stepping onto a floor that might give way, so he changed the subject or simply drifted off, letting his thoughts dissolve into a quiet fantasy world where no one argued and no one watched him.

The memory itself was unpredictable. Some days Amir could not access it deliberately at all: he would sit in his truck after a shift, trying to summon the details, and find only a thick fog. Other days the photograph would flash into his mind without warning—his mother’s eyes, the way her head turned—and his body would react before his mind caught up: his stomach dropped, his shoulders tensed, and the job site around him dissolved into the old kitchen. These sudden intrusions made him more vigilant; he began to read threat into ordinary delays—a supervisor running late meant trouble coming, a slow elevator meant something bad was happening. The world felt charged with impending confrontation, so Amir avoided any situation that might involve disagreement. He stopped eating lunch in the communal trailer, ate alone in his truck instead. When a coworker tried to joke about an argument between two other guys, Amir walked away, his pulse already racing.

This pattern tightened over months. The more he avoided conflict, the more he scanned for threats, and the more he scanned, the more the intrusive memories surfaced. Dwelling on how he used to be—the confident, easygoing version of himself—only deepened the sense that he had lost something essential, and that loss made the future feel meaningless, which in turn made talking about it unbearable. The fantasy escapes became longer; during a safety briefing, he would stare at the unpainted drywall and disappear so completely that the foreman had to tap his shoulder to bring him back. His physical reactions grew stronger, and he began to interpret every flushed face or raised eyebrow as a sign that someone was about to explode.

What finally brought Amir to a clinic was a single moment: a police car pulled into the construction site to check permits, and the sight of the uniform sent him into a full-body panic. He stumbled backward, knocked over a stack of lumber, and had to sit down while the world swam around him. His coworkers stared. The foreman asked if he needed to go home. That night, alone in his apartment, Amir realised he could not keep living inside the loop of avoidance and alarm. He was afraid of what would happen if he tried to break the cycle—afraid that without the scanning and the escape, the memory would overwhelm him completely. But he was more afraid of staying exactly where he was.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat drives or leads to the intrusive memory; threat is described as a consequence of memory or as a trigger for avoidance, but not as a cause of the memory.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, scanning) cause or influence the presence or salience of triggers; triggers are presented as external stimuli that elicit responses, not as outcomes of maladaptive behavior.
